items.title: 68087_Cliff Leeman oral history interview
items.q: Baby Dodds played with the original Three Deuces in 1939 when I had the chance to hear him and to study his approach.

ctx.x: Next to Jo Jones, I would say Sidney Catlett, then possible Zutty Singleton along the way. I'll get to each one eventually. There was Davie Tough, all 110 pounds of him ringing wet! He was a great swinger. And equally as powerful. I have had some people compare my approach to his in a certain period in my life. His was not to predominate the soloist, but to feed them. His big band work with

Woody Herman showed how exciting he could feed without getting in the way of the soloist and the arrangements. I was -- to hear over the years, Baby Dodds, who like Zutty Singleton, came north to Chicago out of New Orleans via the riverboats. Their's was a pulsating, four four beat of the traditional Orleans style. Baby Dodds played with the original Three Deuces in 1939 when I had the chance to hear him and to study his approach.

He worked at the bar with the Deuces with -- did I mention 1939? Yes. He worked with at that time Louie Armstrong on piano and the fabulous -- to me, fabulous -- Lonnie Johnson on guitar, a truly great blues guitarist, blues vocalist. I've been hearing what used to be called race records then, I used to get a hold of everything I could get my hands on, and in that idiom, and I guess that meant predominantly black artists, the race record title that is, because some blue, racy, or possibly offensive material was…
